newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Lufthansa, union prepare for wage showdown.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lufthansa, union prepare for wage showdown.

text.p: Lufthansa AG faces a showdown with its pilots after they gave formal approval to union leaders to call a strike if the German airline does not boost its wage offer.

The DAG union, saying a strike could not be ruled out, on Wednesday said 87 percent of the airline's 3,400 pilots who are union members voted in favour of the strike-authorisation ballot and called on Lufthansa to make a new offer.

But the union suffered a blow when a lack of participation by flight attendants and ground workers in the six-week balloting period meant it failed to reach the quorum needed to give approval for them to participate in any strike action.
Lufthansa said it saw no current strike threat and called on the DAG to return to talks since it said an "overwhelming majority" of its 58,000 workers were against a strike.
But it reaffirmed that it would not change its current offer based on a deal struck late last year with the OeTV union after talks with the DAG had broken off.
The two sides are expected to use a meeting set for Friday in Hamburg to discuss the airline's restructuring programme as a forum to discuss the growing wage conflict as well.
"I think it would be fair to assume that the wage dispute will come up as a topic of discussion after the DAG released the strike ballot votes," a source close to the wage negotiations told Reuters.

Lufthansa has stepped up efforts to isolate union members, saying a strike could put its future in jeopardy. It quoted workers as saying union members should be happy to have jobs at a time of record German unemployment.

The 27-month deal by the OeTV, which represents mainly ground workers, offers a 1.8 percent wage increase in 1998, a one-time payment of one-third of a month's salary and a 500 mark share last year's profit in cash or Lufthansa stock.
Pilots and flight attendants protested against the offer, staging token strikes in November and December that disrupted flights and cost the airline about 30 million marks.

The DAG has demanded a one-year deal as a top priority amid reluctance by union members to get locked into a multi-year contract as the airline seeks to cut costs to improve its competitive stance when European skies are opened in April.

Lufthansa has launched a 1.5 billion mark ($900 million) cost-cutting programme in response to the growing competition, which includes efforts to reduce high German employee costs as well as general operating expenses.
Flight crews have also expressed concern about Lufthansa's plans to hand over some unprofitable routes, such as the Berlin-Frankfurt route, to partner airlines.
The problem is similar to the one which prompted pilots at American Airlines, part of AMR Corp, to strike earlier this month before President Bill Clinton ordered them back to work.

But Lufthansa chief executive Juergen Weber, seeking to reduce high German labour costs, cannot turn to Bonn for help since German law prohibits the government from intervening in a collective-bargaining wage dispute.

Despite the failure of flight attendants and ground workers to give the required 70 percent approval for a strike, a DAG official said a strike by pilots would severely hamper or shut down the carrier since the number of non-union pilots would be insufficient to maintain Lufthansa's worldwide schedule.

In addition, pilot groups at partner airlines of Lufthansa, including United Airlines, South African Airways and Thai Airways, said they would not cross strike lines, casting doubt on whether the pilots would fly aircraft on Lufthansa code-sharing flights.
